articles.text: Classified CSEA workers, a group that includes paraeducators, custodians, and office staff have come to a new agreement with their employer, Piedmont Unified School District. The tentative contract was approved during the April 26 school board meeting; it settles upon salary raises retroactive to the current school year, and the next two years. The contract also includes a one-time payment of $800 for full-time CSEA employees, costing the district $111,000. The three years of cumulative additional salary that CSEA workers will receive is $1,667,000. “The negotiations team and the entire unit saw the wisdom in securing compensation increases and increases in the support for health benefits premiums,” said CSEA President Christine Petersen. The agreement also automatically reopens negotiations if another bargaining party (APT or APSA) gets a “higher percentage ongoing salary or benefit increase or one-time stipend than CSEA.” In this event, the reopening will be for the district to “apply said additional increases” to CSEA classified staff. “We haven’t done multi-year contracts in my entire time on the board,” said Cory Smegal in her 9th year as a member of the school board. “I think what this enables us to do is partner in a different way that will be better for the long-term health of the district.” Additional caveats in the contract will give the CSEA staffers small increases to salary in the event cost of living in the state goes up again. A 0.5% increase to salary would take place if COLA increases by more than 3% in 2024-25 and another 0.5% increase kicks in if COLA exceeds 5% in 2025-26. articles.text: The following letter was sent to Piedmont School Board. Editor: The news and the web are inundated with information about climate change, the bad consequences for the future, and the actions needed. The problem is indeed very serious. Our students are well informed about the issues, some to the point of being traumatized by the fear of an upcoming apocalypse. Given the budget constraints that the District is facing, increasing staff to teach climate literacy could be done to the detriment of other academic subjects, in particular the STEM sciences essential to develop new technologies to decarbonize energy. I would also caution the Board on an approach where climate literacy would be incorporated in every academic subject based on the District previous experience (30?) years ago of mixing the math and physics curriculum: the end result was not much math or physics were taught because every class rehashed the same easy stuff: a unique innovative experiment made by the District that had to be stopped under the pressure from parents. If I remember correctly Martha Jones led the community in the transition and introduced for the first time Advanced Placement classes. Should you decide that such climate literacy education is needed, the best approach would be for the parents pushing the issue to create a group of students passionate about the subject oriented towards experimentation and field activities, such as the very successful and effective Piedmont Makers. Frugality should be part of that group mission statement. There is no easy answer to the warming planet. Our nation does not need more anxious activists, but rather well-educated optimist accountants, entrepreneurs, mathematiciens, engineers, chemists, biologists, ... to develop and implement effective solutions based on a deep understanding of the fundamental laws of physics. –Bernard Pech Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at ­ t ­ t ­ t ­ Mulberry’s Market. articles.text: Climate literacy will be a “hot” topic at the Piedmont Unified School Board meeting on Wednesday, May 8, when a group of students, teachers and parents urges the Board to adopt a Climate Literacy Resolution. The Resolution calls for the District to commit to educating students “for a future with human-induced climate change” by integrating relevant lessons into the curriculum of all subjects at all grade levels, TK-12. According to Moira Chapman, the Piedmont parent who convened the Climate Literacy Working Group last year, “Young people today are concerned with what’s happening to our climate, but they don’t have enough information and skills to fully understand it and adequately prepare for the changes.” “Likewise, many teachers don’t have the training and materials they need to teach about it. The goal of this Resolution is to provide students with a broad knowledge of climate change science, issues, and solutions so they can succeed as the climate changes their future lives and careers.” If the Resolution passes, Piedmont schools will be in line with a new State law, AB 285, that requires science classes in first through 12th grades to “include an emphasis on the causes and effects of climate change and methods to mitigate and adapt to climate change.” The law stipulates that appropriate coursework be offered no later than the 2024– 25 school year. articles.text: Piedmont Fire Department won first place in several key categories at The Big Climb at Oracle Park marking the second consecutive year the department has won the competition overall. Despite being one of the smallest departments in the region, Piedmont Firefighters won several categories in the event’s First Responder Challenge on Saturday, May 4, including “Fastest Team,” “Top Fundraising Team,” and “Fastest Individual Climber.” The Big Climb is a fundraiser for the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society, a national organization dedicated to curing blood cancers and improving the quality of life for patients and their families. Conditions were rainy on the day of the competition, but despite the weather Firefighters Justin McNulty, Anthony Renteria, Niko Christ, Nadder Shehadeh, Christopher Kruger, Brittany Borges, and Brandon Clupny climbed the stadium steps of Oracle Park to a well-deserved, if wet, victory with a team time of 19:47. The Big Climb SF is a competitive stairs race at Oracle Park, where participants compete for time on a course that spans the stadium’s upper deck, descends its ramps, and finishes near the stadium’s second street entrance. On a national level, The Big Climb is hosted at several different stadiums and venues across the country, including Seattle, Dallas, Boston, and Philadelphia. Last year Piedmont won the “Fastest Team” award and its “Fastest Individual Climber” award as part of the First Responder Challenge. Fire Captain Justin McNulty, the department’s principal organizer, took home the “Fastest Individual Climber” award for Piedmont. Last year was the first time The Big Climb included a separate division for first responders, and the new category has already sparked friendly competition among local fire departments. This year, Piedmont competed for the first-place title against other Bay Area fire departments like those of San Francisco and San Mateo. At the time of writing, the Piedmont Fire Department is the sixth-highest corporate donor to the event with $2,180. Overall, the event has raised a total of $175,754 in the LLS. To learn more about the Big Climb in San Francisco and to donate to the Leukemia and Lymphoma Society, visit lls.org/ big-climb. Anthony Renteria (left), Justin McNulty, Niko Christ, Nadder Shehadeh, Christopher Kruger, Brittany Borges, and Brandon Clupny formed the winning team from Piedmont Fire Department at The Big Climb this year.

articles.text: An auto accident near the corner of Park View Avenue and Magnolia Avenue left two vehicles damaged after a driver lost control of the vehicle and struck a parked car on Friday, May 3 around 3:00 p.m. The car flipped onto its side and trapped the driver inside their car, who was eventually rescued by nearby neighbors and responding police officers. No one was injured. Resident John Woodley was gazing out his front window, thinking about work, when he noticed a grey Subaru Forester quickly approaching a stop sign near his house. “It reared up like a horse,” as it entered his vision. The car flipped onto its side, trapping the driver inside. Police Captain Chris Monahan confirmed Woodley’s account. “A Subaru Forester struck a Mini Cooper on its side, which caused the Subaru to flip onto its driver’s side,” explained Monahan. Residents on Park View Avenue who heard the noise quickly gathered around the scene. “About eight neighbors showed up within 30 seconds to attend to the driver who was trapped inside the vehicle,” said Woodley. An airbag had been activated. The driver of the car was an older woman. Within three minutes of the accident, two police cars arrived. had the passenger door open and were using a ladder to help the driver escape. “When I went outside with my phone talking to PPD dispatch, neighbors were communicating with the trapped driver,” said Woodley, who provided his eye-witness account to Detective David Cutler. Overall, three police officers, one community service officer, and eight firefighters responded to the accident. Firefighters examined the driver at the scene for medical reasons, but she requested not to be transported to a hospital. articles.text: Spearheaded by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF), a new flagpole and American flag will soon be installed to honor the late Presiding Justice Carl Anderson. PBF has teamed up with the Piedmont Scout Council and Piedmont Community Church to memorialize the legacy of one of Piedmont’s greatest volunteers who passed away last year. Even while carrying on a distinguished career, first with the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office, then as a Superior Court Judge, a Justice of the California Court of Appeal, and finally as its Presiding Justice, Carl found time to be one of Piedmont’s most important volunteers. Carl’s service on the Piedmont Scout Council was highlighted by his Herculean efforts in concert with Stephen Bechtel Jr. to preserve the Piedmont Council from absorption into a huge Bay Areawide council. Thanks to Carl’s efforts, the Piedmont Council still survives today and is the smallest Council in the national Scouting movement. Throughout his life, Carl was a member of Piedmont Community Church, where he served on many committees, including the Board of Trustees. In his later years, Carl became an Advisor to PBF, offering his wisdom and opening his home for meetings. Opening his home for charitable events was a hallmark of Carl’s approach to giving. Perhaps the greatest highlight in this regard was the unforgettable blessing bestowed upon the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF). He and his wife Margo (who predeceased him) welcomed the PEF to operate from the entire bottom floor of their home for a time of four years. The new flagpole will be located on the Highland Way frontage of the church, near the Scout Office. Local Scouts will be responsible for the management of the American Flag and the location will afford easy access for Scouts working on flag-related requirements for their Tenderfoot and Second-Class ranks. Members of the community who have not yet had an opportunity to honor Carl’s memory are invited to send a contribution to Piedmont Beautification Foundation at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont 94611. Gifts may also be made via PBF’s website, www.piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org. Gifts should be earmarked for the Flagpole Project. Carl’s family will be notified of all gifts made in his honor. PBF has teamed up with the Piedmont Scout Council and Piedmont Community Church to memorialize the legacy of one of Piedmont’s greatest volunteers who passed away last year. Even while carrying on a distinguished career, first with the Alameda County District Attorney’s Office, then as a Superior Court Judge, a Justice of the California Court of Appeal, and finally as its Presiding Justice, Carl found time to be one of Piedmont’s most important volunteers. Carl’s service on the Piedmont Scout Council was highlighted by his Herculean efforts in concert with Stephen Bechtel Jr. to preserve the Piedmont Council from absorption into a huge Bay Areawide council. Thanks to Carl’s efforts, the Piedmont Council still survives today and is the smallest Council in the national Scouting movement. Throughout his life, Carl was a member of Piedmont Community Church, where he served on many committees, including the Board of Trustees. In his later years, Carl became an Advisor to PBF, offering his wisdom and opening his home for meetings. Opening his home for charitable events was a hallmark of Carl’s approach to giving. Perhaps the greatest highlight in this regard was the unforgettable blessing bestowed upon the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF). He and his wife Margo (who predeceased him) welcomed the PEF to operate from the entire bottom floor of their home for a time of four years. The new flagpole will be located on the Highland Way frontage of the church, near the Scout Office. Local Scouts will be responsible for the management of the American Flag and the location will afford easy access for Scouts working on flag-related requirements for their Tenderfoot and Second-Class ranks. Members of the community who have not yet had an opportunity to honor Carl’s memory are invited to send a contribution to Piedmont Beautification Foundation at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Ave., Piedmont 94611. articles.text: On the weekend of Sunday, April 21, the Recreation Department invited families to enjoy a free afternoon of homemade miniature golf courses at the first Pop-Up Putt Putt in Piedmont. Beginning at noon in the Community Hall parking lot, more than 260 community members played on 15 courses, 10 designed by Rec Dept. employees and another five by the public. Awards were given for “Best Overall Course,” “Most Creative Course,” “Most Clever Course,” “Best Use of Recycled Materials,” “Best Kid Theme,” and a category dubbed “Sooo Piedmont,” – for embodying the town’s spirit. Although the mini-golf activities were the main attraction, attendees also entertained themselves by enjoying picnic lunches on the lawn and listening to music. ACE Kids, an East Bay junior golf program, also brought a mobile golf simulator so participants could try their skills in a more controlled environment. And the winners are. . . • Best Overall: “House on the Green” by Akil Danjuma, Sports Coordinator at the PRD • Most Creative: “Sneaky Tiki” by Woody Miller Art & The Miller/Murphy Family • Most Clever: “Piedmont Pinball Putt-Putt” by Nicole Verhalen • Best Use of Recycled Materials: “Magnolia Avenue” by Piedmont Recreation Commissioners Jenny Feinberg and Dick Carter • Sooo Piedmont: “Piedmont is the G.O.A.T” by the Pike/Phillips Family • Best Kid Theme: “Pee-Wee Fairway” by Very Barry Labs Winners were recognized at the May 6 City Council meeting. “Overall, this was a wonderful and free family-friendly event,” said Rec Director Chelle Putzer. “PRD would like to thank all of the community members who created a hole for the course, ACE Golf, and PRD’s very own DJ Kev for spinnin’ tunes in the Park!” The “Magic is our Mojo” course created by the Piedmont Recreation Department for the event. articles.text: The Piedmont School Board meeting tonight, May 8, will be held in City Hall at 7:00 p.m., and will include important items for the future of Piedmont schools. articles.text: The busy Piedmont High School and Middle School instrumental music programs bring the school year to an end with three wonderful May concerts at the Alan Harvey Theater, beginning Tuesday, May 21st. Tuesday, May 21, 7:00 p.m. The PHS Symphonic Band & Jazz Band, directed by Band teacher Trevor Meseroll, will present a combined Spring Concert. The evening will include music by Stevie Wonder and Barry Manilow, selections from the movie Pirates of the Caribbean, “Agua De Beber” by Antonio Carlos Jobim, and the jazz standard “Unforgettable” with vocal soloist Nate McKenzie. Several small jazz combos will also be on the program. Wednesday, May 22, 7:00 p.m. The PMS 7th grade and 8th grade bands led by Meseroll and the 6th grade band led by Cathy DeVos (6th grade) take the stage. Included on the program is music by Freddie Mercury, Bruno Mars, and the rock band Chicago. A calypso piece, as well as a March and an Overture by Bruce Pearson, will appear on the program. Well-known musical standards such as “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough” and “Saturday in the Park” will also be performed. Thursday, May 23, at 7:00 p.m. The PMS & PHS Orchestras, directed by Sam Wilde, take their turn on the Alan Harvey Theater stage. Music selections on the PMS program include “Viva la Vida” by Coldplay and music from the movie “The Hunger Games.” The PHS High School Orchestra repertoire includes the gorgeous Edward Elgar piece “Nimrod,” the first movement of Franz Schubert’s Symphony #5, and music from “Scheherazade” by Rimsky-Korsakov, which is based on the tales of the Arabian Nights. To help offset concert expenses at all concerts, a $5.00 suggested donation for adults will be requested at the door. All students are admitted free.

articles.text: Deanna Johnson, Director of Highlands Preschool, has announced her plans to retire at the end of the school year after 25 years of teaching. Johnson began at Highlands in 1999 as a parttime classroom assistant and now, 750 students later, she retiring. Johnson has been involved with children in some capacity for over 40 years whether as a babysitter, nanny, camp counselor, reading coach, teacher or preschool director. “I have learned so much in my 25 years at Highlands. As teachers, we have the amazing, unique privilege of helping children discover who they are and develop a love of learning. It is a privilege to impact their lives in a positive way,” said Johnson. Johnson’s history in the Piedmont community goes back to Wildwood Elementary, where she attended school as a kid and then later graduated from Piedmont High. Some of her favorite memories growing up include exploring the creek and caves in Piedmont Park, and riding her bike around Witter Field. Johnson has had a significant Deanna Johnson playing dress up with a preschool student. impact on the community and can be spotted by her huge smile, infectious laugh, and unmistakable rapport with children. “[Children] are pure and genuine and are full of boundless energy and creativity. They help remind me to see things as they do: with wonder, excitement and awe,” she said. Johnson will stay on next year as advisor. Angela Livermore, who has been teaching at Highlands for 15 years, will become the school’s new director. “I have been so lucky to work for so long at a job that I love. There is truly a special feeling at Highlands. It’s magical, and I know that whatever I do in my life, I’ll take a little bit of that magic with me,” said Johnson. articles.text: A Scout is many things (Trustworthy, Loyal, Helpful, Friendly, Courteous, Kind, Obedient, Cheerful, Thrifty, Brave, Clean, and Reverent); and Eagle Scouts work very hard over many years to earn their ranks. On Friday, May 10, five deserving young men and women from the Piedmont Scout Council Troop 11 were presented their Eagle Scout ranks in a ceremony at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse at Havens Elementary. The evening was filled with ceremony enough to inspire all the younger scouts towards the rank of Eagle. Earning the rank of Eagle takes years of devoted work and six ranks to qualify to start the Eagle requirements. Each rank has requirements that teach skills and leadership, until the Scouts are in active leadership roles for their unit. They participate as troop leaders for at least 16 months, and have seven boards of review, seven scoutmaster conferences, while volunteering time in the community and for the council. The goal is to teach them to be leaders in society with the award of Eagle, a rank widely being regarded by political, military, and business leaders to be a sign of special leadership skills. While earning ranks, each candidate must also earn at least 21 merit badges. Another requirement is to propose, get approved, then conduct an Eagle project that benefits their community. The current group of five have collectively contributed many hundreds of community hours from collecting food at Scouting for Food to their Eagle projects. They also have helped fund their council through their efforts supporting the annual Christmas tree lot. The Piedmont Scout Council is the smallest council in the United States, thriving in a small, tightknit community. Being small has its advantages. Nationally, only a very small percentage become Eagle, whereas the Piedmont Council’s program has a much higher percentage. Each year, about 100 scouts or more enter the program and about 20 Eagle ranks are awarded. Piedmont also benefits from a much higher percentage of saturation within our community. About 25% of available youth participate in Piedmont, as compared with the national average of 2%. Each of the five new Eagles has gone on many outings from ski trips, snow camping trips, rafting, and canoeing trips to competitive events that demonstrate and test their outdoor and leadership skills. They’ve spent time in rain-soaked tents and learning hard lessons about how to survive and thrive in all conditions. Each of them has cooked their meals over open fires and spent their nights among the wildlife that they try to respect and preserve. articles.text: Emily Thompson The end of the school year is fast approaching, and this time of year can be particularly stressful. On top of preparing for finals, many students are also taking AP exams, managing extracurricular activities, making college visits, and planning their summers. It is important to think about tangible ways students can navigate this stressful time. Below are three action items that we have found particularly useful in helping students manage their stress: • Take care of yourself When we feel stressed, selfcare is often the first thing we sacrifice. It is imperative that students prioritize sleep, healthy diet, and exercise. The brain’s ability to learn and store information improves when well-rested and well-fed. Exercise helps reduce stress hormones, like cortisol and adrenaline, which negatively impact our ability to concentrate. While staying up until 3 a.m. to cram for an exam might seem like a good idea at the time, it is likely counterproductive. • Make a plan Write out a thorough list that includes the dates of academic items (assignments and tests) as well as non-academic priorities (like an important track meet or a friend’s bat mitzvah). Creating a timeline of events makes it easier to understand what the top priorities are and what steps to take, which helps combat the feeling of overwhelm when it is unclear where to start. • Set realistic goals Have you heard of SMART goals? SMART goals are a game-changer for many students. SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Rather than setting a vague goal to “study” for your biology final, here is an example of a SMART goal: “locate my biology study guide and organize my class notes by Tuesday; spend one hour reviewing my flashcards on Wednesday; complete the extra practice problems and review my misses on Thursday.” specific and manageable chunks, students have a better chance of holding themselves accountable and reaching their goals. Managing stress is about building better habits! While this time of year is particularly hectic, these tips can help mitigate stress for students (and adults!) any time the to-do list feels daunting. Ariel Rodriguez is the Director of College Counseling and Emily is the Managing Director at Study Smarter. pages.text: Wednesday, May 8, 2024 11 Thinking Outside the Classroom Helping students manage stress By Ariel Rodriguez and Emily Thompson The end of the school year is fast approaching, and this time of year can be particularly stressful. On top of preparing for finals, many students are also taking AP exams, managing extracurricular activities, making college visits, and planning their summers. It is important to think about tangible ways students can navigate this stressful time. Below are three action items that we have found particularly useful in helping students manage their stress: • Take care of yourself When we feel stressed, selfcare is often the first thing we sacrifice. It is imperative that students prioritize sleep, healthy diet, and exercise. The brain’s ability to learn and store information improves when well-rested and well-fed. Exercise helps reduce stress hormones, like cortisol and adrenaline, which negatively impact our ability to concentrate. While staying up until 3 a.m. to cram for an exam might seem like a good idea at the time, it is likely counterproductive. • Make a plan Write out a thorough list that includes the dates of academic items (assignments and tests) as well as non-academic priorities (like an important track meet or a friend’s bat mitzvah). Creating a timeline of events makes it easier to understand what the top priorities are and what steps to take, which helps combat the feeling of overwhelm when it is unclear where to start. • Set realistic goals Have you heard of SMART goals? SMART goals are a game-changer for many students. SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. Rather than setting a vague goal to “study” for your biology final, here is an example of a SMART goal: “locate my biology study guide and organize my class notes by Tuesday; spend one hour reviewing my flashcards on Wednesday; complete the extra practice problems and review my misses on Thursday.” By breaking the goal into more specific and manageable chunks, students have a better chance of holding themselves accountable and reaching their goals. Managing stress is about building better habits! While this time of year is particularly hectic, these tips can help mitigate stress for students (and adults!) any time the to-do list feels daunting. articles.text: Photo by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team gathers for one last photo following their NCS Quarterfinals match. The Highlanders’ girls’ lacrosse team had its season come to an end on Thursday, May 2 with a 9-7 loss to No. 4 Acalanes in Lafayette in the North Coast Section quarterfinals. PHS earlier defeated No. 12 Urban 20-5 in the first round on Tuesday, April 30 at Witter Field. Thursday’s game featured Piedmont responding to a fivegoal deficit in the third quarter when trailing 6-1. “At the end of the day, it was just landing our shots. We were getting our plays, we were getting shooting space chances, everything was coming together. Their goalie was amazing, so hat’s off to her. We just told them to make a slight adjustment in their shot to shoot it at her foot, or make the ball bounce about a foot in front of her, and it was beautiful to see the team execute that slight adjustment,” coach Carlton Chan said. Acalanes’ last line of defense ultimately made the difference with goalie Addie Martin recording 11 saves. Senior attacker Ruby Guzdar was a major part of the Highlanders’ turnaround, scoring four goals in the second half. “Their goalie was very good and was saving our usual shots. But we knew in the second quarter that if we falter this way and give in, this would be it and we’re going to go home feeling sad knowing we could’ve played better. We turned on the gas at the end,” Guzdar said. Winning face offs was a big factor in the Piedmont comeback rally, in which they scored five straight goals after winning draws in the third- and fourth-quarters. Senior midfielder Hailey Marshburn grabbed four draws while and Hallie Burden won six. “A big thing was the draws. We started winning those draws and it’s a big confidence boost because you have possession and it gives you an opportunity to make something of it on the offensive end,” said Marshburn. articles.text: Piedmont High sophomore Lucas Smolko battled his way to the semifinals of the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tennis Tournament at Golden Gate Park in San Francisco on Friday and Monday, May 3-6. Despite playing strong tennis on the opening day of the tournament, Smolko had to retire during the second set of his match against University’s eventual-champion Karam Dhawan due to illness. Smolko dropped the first set 6-3 and was down 4-0 in the second set. He earned fourth-place in singles. “Lucas was playing great on Friday and had two dominant wins. But on Monday, he was sick and had to retire in the second set of his match against Karam Dhawan,” explained coach Jim Landes. Karam went on to win the championship over Lick-Wilmerding’s Saahil Mishra,” Smolko defeated Mishra, the finalist from Lick, earlier this season 6-1, 7-6 (7-3) on March 13. On Friday, Smolko won his opening round match over Davis Walsh of Cardinal Newman in straight sets, 6-1, 6-1. He followed up with a dominant 6-0, 6-3 win over Rex Rutchik of Marin Academy in the quarterfinals. It’s an unfortunate turn for Lucas after entering the tournament with the No. 1 seed. The Highlanders clinched the top seed with a 7-5 win over Berkeley in extra innings on Wednesday, May 1 in Berkeley. Two days later, the Yellowjackets won in another high-scoring game, 8-6. On Tuesday, Piedmont took an early 2-0 lead but Alameda tied it at 2-2 and the game waged scoreless until the Hornets went ahead in the top of the eighth. Although the Highlanders finished the regular season in first place, they needed a championship victory in the WACC Tournament to secure an automatic home playoff bid for the firstround of the North Coast Section playoffs next week. 4-2 to Alameda Piedmont opened scoring with two runs in the bottom of the second, but Alameda tacked on two runs in the top of the third. The score continued scoreless until the Hornets scored two runs in the top of the eighth inning. Starting pitcher Seve Sanchez powered 5.1 winnings for four strikeouts and allowed just one earned run. Alameda’s Max Cohen threw seven innings after entering in the second, throwing over 100 pitches until Cole Aney closed out the game. Piedmont upset by Alameda in league semifinals PHS fought valiantly in the bottom eighth, scoring once in a two-out rally when Peter Krumins singled in Will Parker, but they fell short. Final stats: Krumins was 1-for-3 with an RBI and run scored. Markos Lagios went 1-for-4, Diego Delventhal was 1-for-4, Parker was 1-for-4 with a double, Shafer Dando was 2-for-3 with a double and one RBI. 7-5 win over Berkeley Berkeley scored in the bottom of the first, but PHS went ahead 2-1 after the top of the second and added one more in the top of the third. BHS tied 3-3 in the bottom third, but Piedmont scored successive runs in the top of the fourth and fifth innings, up 5-3. Berkeley scored twice in the bottom fifth to knot it up at 5-all. After both teams went scoreless in the seventh and eighth, PHS went ahead with a pair of runs in the top of the ninth. Jack Meyjes was the winning pitcher, throwing the final four innings. He closed out the game with two strikeouts in the ninth inning. Peter Krumins cracked a one-run home run in the top of the fifth. PHS scored the go-ahead in the top of the ninth after Will Parker advanced to third on a wild pitch, then Shafer Dando reached first on an error that also allowed Parker to score. Krumins scored with two outs on an error by the catcher with Jordan Vo at bat. Final stats: Parker hit 2-for-4, Krumins was 2-for-3 with a home run, two RBIs, two runs scored, and two walks. Dando was 1-for-4 with a double, one run and an RBI. Vo was 2-for-4 with two RBIs. Meyjes had an RBI as well. Staff Photos Seve Sanchez pitched 5.1 innings of stellar baseball, striking out four and allowing three hits and only one earned run. 8-6 to Berkeley Piedmont led 2-0 after the bottom of the second, but allowed two runs in the top of the third and three in the top fourth. PHS tied 6-6 lead with a four-run bottom of the sixth, but Berkeley scored twice in the top of the seventh. Dimitri Papahadjopoulos smacked a two-run homer in the bottom of the second. Final stats: Brandon Dicke went 1-for-3. Krumins was 1-for-3 with a double and two runs scored. Papahadjopoulos was 1-for-3 with a home run, two RBIs and a run. Parker was 1-for-2 with an RBI and run scored. Meyjes was 1-for-3 with two RBIs. NEXT UP Piedmont (15-8 overall) hosts the winner of Castro Valley and Bishop O’Dowd on Thursday, May 9. Smolko reaches NCS Individual semifinals By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High sophomore Lucas Smolko battled his way to the semifinals of the Division 2 North Coast Section Individual Tennis Tournament at Golden Gate Park in San Francisco on Friday and Monday, May 3-6. Despite playing strong tennis on the opening day of the tournament, Smolko had to retire during the second set of his match against University’s eventual-champion Karam Dhawan due to illness. Smolko dropped the first set 6-3 and was down 4-0 in the second set. He earned fourth-place in singles. “Lucas was playing great on Friday and had two dominant wins. But on Monday, he was sick and had to retire in the second set of his match against Karam Dhawan,” explained coach Jim Landes. Karam went on to win the championship over Lick-Wilmerding’s Saahil Mishra,” Smolko defeated Mishra, the finalist from Lick, earlier this season 6-1, 7-6 (7-3) on March 13. On Friday, Smolko won his opening round match over Davis Walsh of Cardinal Newman in straight sets, 6-1, 6-1. He followed up with a dominant 6-0, 6-3 win over Rex Rutchik of Marin Academy in the quarterfinals. It’s an unfortunate turn for Lucas after entering the tournament with the No. 1 seed. He came to NCS after winning this year’s league championship singles title the previous week. Also competing in the singles ladder was Piedmont senior Ben Breber, falling to Mishra 6-1, 6-0 in the first round. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse’s season came to an end on Tuesday, April 30 in the first-round of the Division 1 North Coast Section playoffs. Seeded No. 11, they lost 15-7 loss at No. 6 San Ramon Valley in Danville. The loss concludes PHS’ season with an 8-6 overall record. Despite a productive start against SRV with five goals in the first quarter to trail 8-5 after a high-scoring opening 12 minutes, the Highlanders’ attack couldn’t find the same fluidity as the early going and managed to score just two goals in the remaining three quarters. It was a rough transition year for Piedmont High. They school didn’t secure a league title for the first time after six consecutive years as Western Alameda County Conference champions. PHS earned a promotion to NCS’ top division after reaching last year’s D2 NCS Finals, which they lost 9-8 in sudden-death overtime to Tamalpais. But shortly after last year’s Finals, coach Al Yu and assistant coaches David Hafner and Matt Palasek announced they were departing after the season. Palasek elected to stay closer to home to become Casa Grande’s head coach, which made it to the NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 8 seed before losing to No. 1 Marin Catholic. PHS freshman Connor Fredericks was a standout player in his debut year. Staff Photos Rylan Nelson scored three goals in his final Piedmont appearance. However, online records show Piedmont never prepared for Yu’s departure. The job opening was not posted on Edjoin.com until November. And with a lack of available lacrosse coaches in the area, Piedmont parents scrambled to find new coach Jeff Lamb through a personal connection just months before the season started. Despite Lamb’s lack of time in a coaching role, this year’s team was able to lean on the experience of Rylan Nelson, Curtis Hohener, Oliver Shafroth, Andrew Mclaughlin, Keita Clear, Logan Huh, and Gus Von Metzsch, while also identifying a standout freshman, Connor Fredericks. They established a sixgame winning streak in March to create a 6-2 record and even recorded their first shutout of a D1 opponent in a 7-0 win over Cal High on March 8. The last time Piedmont was in D1, they lost 21-7 to No. 4 Vista Del Lago in 2022 as the No. 13 seed. The next season, PHS returned to D2 to narrowly lose the Finals to No. 1 Tamalpais 9-8 as the No. 3 seed. It will be interesting to see if PHS will return to D2 in 2025. 15-7 to San Ramon Valley Piedmont trailed San Ramon Valley 8-5 after a high scoring first quarter, but the Wolves jumped out to an 11-5 lead in the second quarter by netting six and not allowing a single goal. PHS scored once in the third and once in the fourth. In the first quarter, San Ramon Valley won the opening face off and scored 30 seconds into the match. But Piedmont returned the favor on the next faceoff, with Fredericks winning the draw before Shafroth scored after just 12 seconds, 1-1 at 11:20. PHS then took a 2-1 lead with a shot by Nelson in transition after winning the faceoff for a goal just 13 seconds later. Shafroth then put PHS ahead 3-1 with 9:12 on the clock. But from there, SRV went on a three goal scoring run to lead 4-3 at the 4:07 mark. Timmy Kalamas tied it up for Piedmont at 2:35, but San Ramon Valley fired off another three goals in rapid fire succession to lead 7-4 with 44.5 seconds left. Nelson then drew it closed with a goal with 23 seconds left, but SRV won the following faceoff and scored right before halftime, 8-5. That was the closest things got for the Highlanders, going scoreless in the second quarter but allowing three. Nelson scored once in the third quarter, while Shafroth got one in the fourth. Final stats: Nelson had three goals and grabbed three ground balls. Shafroth also scored three, had one assist, and gathered three loose balls. Kalamas scored once. Fredericks grabbed four ground balls and won seven draws. Von Metszch had 14 saves. Senior Oliver Shafroth has a hat trick for Piedmont.

articles.text: Nina Schwab qualifies for CIF State On May 3 Piedmont High’s swim team competed at the Concord Community Pool for the preliminary round of this year’s North Coast Section Championship. The top 40 swimmers in the section competed to determine which 16 would move on to the NCS finals on Friday May 4. Piedmont’s only diver, senior Nina Schwab, qualified for the CIF State Championship by finishing fourth out of 16 divers for the one-meter dive with a score of 423.75 after 11 dives. She’ll travel to Clovis West High School in Fresno for the State Diving Championship on May 9-11. The weather was a drastic change from Friday’s sunny and warm prelims, with temps all Saturday in the mid 50’s, and heavy rain. As a result, almost all swimmers had slower times than the previous day. In the NCS finals Owen Blanford placed ninth of 16 in the 200 Free with a time of 1:42.58. His time was fast enough to gain a CIF Consideration listing, making him an alternate at State. The boys’ 200 Free Relay of Blanford, Tom Rolefson, Nik Costello and Dima Secor placed 11th of 16 teams with a time of 1:28.23, gaining them a CIF Consideration time. To get there, the squad was 13th of 40 in the prelims in 1:27.79 which is a PHS record. PHS’ boys 400 Free Relay of Blanford, Rolefson, Costello, and Asher Takazawa were also 11th of 16 with a time of 3:11.66 to gain a CIF State Consideration as well. They reached the finals by finishing ninth of 40 in the prelims in 3:10.09. Both the 200 and 400 freestyle relay teams will be alternatives for State. Asher Takazawa was 16th in the 100 backstroke with a time of 54.25. He qualified for the finals by finishing 17th of 40 in 53.03. For the girls, Taylor Rolefson placed 16th in the 100 butterfly in 59.73. She reached the finals by finishing 16th of 40 in the preliminaries, 58.44. Piedmont’s softball team battled in the first-round of the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Tournament as the No. 5 seed against No. 4 San Leandro on Monday, May 6 at Burrell Field. After trailing 2-1 through the first four innings, San Leandro piled on six runs in the bottom of the fourth and another three in the bottom of the fifth to activate the 10-run rule and win 11-1. PHS was looking productive in its first four innings of work with Miya Fujimoto on the mound. Prior to exiting after three innings of pitching, Fujimoto had seven strikeouts. However, the junior leader twisted her ankle in the top of the fourth on first base after hitting a fielder’s choice groundball. Although Fujimoto is naturally an infielder and ideally plays shortstop as Piedmont’s best glove in the field, she’s pitched for the Highlanders over the past two years. Aside from her, PHS doesn’t have anyone with pitching experience. “Fuji got hurt and the momentum went downhill. She’s been the biggest part of the team all year, she’s thrown at least 100 innings for us in her two years as a pitcher. She’s been our ace and she’s not a pitcher, that’s the thing about it. But she’s pitching for the team and I appreciate that. These girls are giving it their all, and that’s all I can ask for,” coach Gene Denard said following the game. It was an inauspicious start for Piedmont High. Already short on players, the beginning of the game had to be halted with students late to the field due to ongoing testing around this time of the year. With just 11 players on the roster, Fujimoto’s injury exasperated an already depleted lineup. “Today just started bad, there was some miscommunication about testing and had to wait for players to come. It was a bad omen for the day, then Fuji gets hurt in an inning where it looks like we’re going to score about four runs,” Denard said. This year’s WACC Shoreline tournament was structured differently than other years, including the last time PHS won the division in 2022. articles.text: Visit the Oakland Museum of California this Saturday, May 11, for a curated gallery chat focused on Asian American and Pacific Islander history. Curated by longtime museum volunteer and former teacher Margaret Yee, this event presents an opportunity to share questions and reflections on key moments in California Asian American history and explore how the causes and consequences of these events still reverberate today. Yee has been volunteering at OMCA since 2017, first as a history gallery docent and now as a School Programs and Gallery Chats Facilitator. The event is free for museum members and begins at 12 p.m. To learn more, visit https://museumca.org/event/member-gallery-chats-california-aapi-history/.

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco’s newest exhibition, entitled !!!!!, is on view now through September. The exhibition features artwork by British visual artist and painter Rachel Jones, known for her use of vivid oil pastel landscapes and exploration into Black interiority and personhood. Jones studied at Glasgow School of Art and graduated in 2013. She then earned her Masters in Fine Art at the Royal Academy Schools, London, in 2019. Recent solo exhibitions include the Long Museum, Shanghai, China (2023) and the Chisenhale Gallery, London (2022). This is the first solo museum exhibition for Jones in the United States. In this exhibition, Jones is inspired by the poetics of Black writers and the visual languages of cartoons, through her signature medium of oil pastels. The artist said she is “using motifs and color as a way to communicate ideas about the interiority Rachel Jones of Black bodies and their lived experience.” For more information, and to purchase tickets to MoAD, visit https://www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/rachel-jones.
articles.title: MoAD presents new exhibition

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek will host a fundraising gala on Saturday, May 18 at 5 p.m. Guests are invited to immerse themselves in the vibrant beauty of South Africa’s dry garden landscape while enjoying a relaxed, outdoor affair with refreshments and live music. Curators will share insights into the drought-tolerant and climate-adaptive plants within Ruth’s collection. Ruth Bancroft, the nursery’s namesake and founder, was ahead of her time in her focus on conservative gardening and drought-tolerant plants. The mission of the Ruth Bancroft Gardens is to preserve her garden for the education and enjoyment of the public, made possible through fundraising events like this. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/ gala/. Gala guests are invited to enjoy live music and drinks in Ruth Bancroft Gardens. By Allyson Aleksey The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco’s newest exhibition, entitled !!!!!, is on view now through September. The exhibition features artwork by British visual artist and painter Rachel Jones, known for her use of vivid oil pastel landscapes and exploration into Black interiority and personhood. Jones studied at Glasgow School of Art and graduated in 2013. She then earned her Masters in Fine Art at the Royal Academy Schools, London, in 2019. Recent solo exhibitions include the Long Museum, Shanghai, China (2023) and the Chisenhale Gallery, London (2022). This is the first solo museum exhibition for Jones in the United States. In this exhibition, Jones is inspired by the poetics of Black writers and the visual languages of cartoons, through her signature medium of oil pastels. articles.text: Monika Gruber, Omid Assadi, David Wishnia and David Ryther of the Circadian String Quartet Circadian String Quartet performs its first concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on May 24 at 7:30 pm. Titled Love and Chains, the concert includes special guests Leslie Bonnet and Nikolaus Hohmann. Tickets are $25 general/$15 seniors and students and are available at www.eventbrite. com/e/894985956087. The concert explores the deep bonds and binds that come with Love. Experience the world premiere of an original chamber opera, Euridice’s Defiance, composed by David Ryther. Inspired by the Greek myth of Orpheus and Euridice, this work in progress tells the story of a mother, Euridice, being detained at a border crossing and separated from her son, Orpheus, while she pleads with her guard to re-unite them. The ground-breaking libretto, written by novelist Kimiko Guthrie, is set to a haunting score by Ryther. The concert will also include Preludes by Claude Debussy, arranged for string quartet; Anton Webern’s romantic opus Langsamer Satz, and two works by Iranian-born composer Sahba Aminikia which are profound meditations on geopolitical struggles that are born from the love of our common humanity.

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s 2024 Summer Season opens on May 30 with Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s The Magic Flute, one of the last operas the composer completed before his death in 1791. San Francisco Opera Director Eun Sun Kim teams with producers Barrie Kosky and Suzanne Andrade to bring Mozart’s beloved opera to life, drawing inspiration from the art of silent film, early Hollywood animation and 1920’s Berlin cabaret. Kim conducted The Magic Flute with multiple European companies as well as the Washington National Opera and will now lead the San Francisco Opera’s first presentation in nearly a decade. The performers include New Zealand-Samoan tenor Amitai Pati as Tamino and Austrian soprano Christina Gansch as Pamina. The international cast also features Estonian bass-baritone Lauri Vasar as Papageno, South Korean bass Kwangchul Youn as Sarastro, and Polish soprano Anna Simińska as the Queen of the Night. Sung in German with English supertitles, the nine performances of The Magic Flute are scheduled for May 30 (7:30 p.m.); June 2 (2 p.m.), 4 (7:30 p.m.), 8 (7:30 p.m.), 14 (7:30 p.m.), 20 (7:30 p.m.), 22 (7:30 p.m.), 26 (7:30 p.m.), 30 (2 p.m.). To purchase tickets, visit www.sfopera.com. Playbill cover for San Francisco Opera’s production of The Magic Flute.

But, all of his other musical attributes more than compensated for stentorian dynamics. And now for some food As good as these musical events were, the real treat was dinner at a friend’s house on Friday evening. Our friend, Doug, is very modest about his abilities in the kitchen. His main course of stuffed chicken breast served alongside a bulgur wheat pilaf would be the featured item in any fancy restaurant. What made it even more amazing was that it is very easy to prepare. Doug prefers to use skinless chicken breast with one large breast for two people. First, he pounds it to tenderize it and to reduce its thickness. Add a little salt and pepper to the outside and stuff it with red peppers from a jar and some mozzarella cheese. He uses mozzarella cheese because it will not run when heated. Stuff the chicken breast and tie it with some kitchen string. Brown the chicken breasts in a little bit of butter using a cast-iron skillet. Then place the entire cast-iron skillet into a preheated 400° oven. Cook for about 10 minutes. Take it out, and let it rest for a few minutes, then slice it. That’s it. Beautiful and tasty – and very simple to prepare. The sliced chicken breasts were served with a simple bulgur wheat pilaf. Doug is also very modest about his knowledge of wines. He served a simple, dry red wine: a Merlot. As if that were not enough, Doug then played a brief concert for us on the piano. The view of the San Francisco Bay, combined with the delicious food and the music, made for a very memorable evening. articles.text: The Dinner, set in a five-star, chic restaurant, where the many courses are presented with a monologue, is a film of humid At first it appears to be merely four people meeting for a meal – two brothers, Stan (Richard Gere), Paul (Steve Coogan) and their wives, Claire (Laura Linney) and Katelyn (Rebecca Hall). What quickly becomes obvious is that they arrive with more baggage than a hotel lobby, meaning unresolved issues that for Stan and Paul stretch back to their youth. It’s clear that Paul is dragging with him through life, like a wet sack of cement, anger and resentment and grievances that he insists were not of his He actually snarls to Stan, “Mom loved you more.” Stan is a successful congressman; Paul was once a high school history teacher now apparently unemployed. Katelyn is Stan’s second wife (previously a campaign aide). Claire is, beyond all understanding, a caring wife to Paul and not that long ago out of the hospital after recovering from Paul is a loose cannon on the dinner table deck, acerbically reactive, his language raw and vitriolic, perpetually skirting full-blown rage or on the verge of losing it altogether, contributing massively to the sustained tension. Through flashbacks, A scene from The Dinner with Richard Gere, Laura Linney, Steve Coogan, and Rebecca Hall which are used sparingly but to excellent effect, we’re told that he has suffered from a mental breakdown and clearly remains fragile and conflicted about all of his connections, especially to his brother. Contributing to the cognitive dissonance that grips the brittle dinner conversation is the arrival of their haute cuisine that remains, in great part, uneaten. What is really being served is Stan’s motivation for bringing them together. I am reluctant to explain in too much detail what has occurred, but suffice it to say that it involves the couples’ sons, both 16, who are involved in a horrific act. Stan insists that they, meaning all four of them, must confront what has occurred and make a decision as to how to proceed. He argues that if they fail to deal with this event, their lives will be ruined. He means all of their lives. Most especially the boys. What also becomes evident is that their inherent dysfunction is only intensified for there is nothing in any of their experiences that could prepare them for this crossroads moment. Of course they are flawed, haunted by their imperfections and therefore starkly ill-equipped to form any kind of a united front. The question to be asked is whether a movie such as this find an audience. It is a long and disjointed hothouse of conversation; however, it’s also a tour de force of acting by an ensemble that is remarkable. The Dinner. Directed by Oren Moverman. articles.text: The Edge of Seventeen is perhaps one of the best movies about adolescent angst and coming of age in the last 25 years. It’s that good. To write and direct a film that captures the essence of being 17, meaning that profound feeling that your life is unmoored and uncertain, feeling at a loss to explain the buffeting emotions that seem like a cascade of conflicting impulses that can rule one’s life; well, that is no small thing. Director Kelly Fremon Craig gets it just right, avoiding a minefield of clichés. At the center of Edge is Nadine (Hailee Steinfeld), suffering with a perfect storm of emotions. Several years ago she lost her father, to whom she was especially close. And now her best friend since childhood, Krista (Haley Lu Richardson), has fallen for Darian (Blake Jenner), her older, eternally perfect and popular brother. Nadine feels abruptly rejected and betrayed and so banishes Krista from her life. Suddenly rudderless, friendless, and convinced she is utterly alone, she decides to kill herself (or imagines she will.) During lunch hour she informs Mr. Bruner (a remarkably good Woody Harrelson), her history teacher, of her intention. While Nadine is a master of histrionics and self-absorbed drama, the laconic and dry Mr. Bruner Hailee Steinfeld stars in The Edge of Seventeen.
articles.title: The Edge of Seventeen a superb coming-of-age film

articles.text: The premise of Wreck-It Ralph is not only retro, but decidedly creative and fun. The story is set in a suburban arcade filled with games, a place where the neighborhood cool kids hangout during the day. But here’s the best part: when the arcade shuts down for the night, and the kids have all gone home, it’s transformed into an enchanting world where the game characters cross-over into each others platforms and, well, socialize. One of the video game meanies is Wreck-It-Ralph (John C. Reilly), a nemesis in a game called Fix-It-Felix Jr. Ralph is a big, hulking guy with oversized hands and feet who smashes up buildings while Felix (Jack Brayer) follows closely behind with his magic hammer, repairing the damage. Ralph has been wrecking the same building for years, day after day. Of course, he always faces the threat of the Newlanders, hostile residents who live in the building Ralph is wrecking. Meanwhile, Ralph sleeps in a garbage dump when he’s not wrecking stuff, using a tree stump for a pillow. For Ralph, it’s a lonely, sad life, and he wants out. So Ralph abandons his game to try out others. The problem is that when he doesn’t return the kids think Fix-It-Felix Jr. is broken. Felix is therefore desperate to find Ralph and get him to come back so he’ll have things to fix. Meanwhile, Ralph is wandering from game to game. As it turns out, he spends a lot of time in a game called Sugar Rush where he becomes friends with Vanellope von Schweetz (Sarah Silverman) who has been prevented by despot King Candy and a group of mean girls from competing in the go-cart races. Both Vanellope and Ralph are unhappy and want to break free of their games’ programs. The story has a nice finale, involving the gateway to the inner arcade, called Arcade Central, while introducing a bevy of characters. There are also lots of stops along the way, some involving secret passages, cheat codes, and restarts. Plus, the point is made that the arcade characters work long hours, all for the kids’ pleasure. Wreck-It Ralph has wonderful visuals, and Ralph is actually likable and charming. The jokes are silly in a nice way, and it’s a treat to follow Ralph on his journey to leave behind his old meanie role of breaking stuff. Ditto Vanellope von Schweetz. Wreck-It Ralph. articles.text: A scene from Raya and the Last Dragon Raya and the Last Dragon is a family friendly, action adventure tale that will resonate with young audiences. Its animation is extraordinary and has been judged to be some of Disney’s best work. The setting is a wonderfully imagined region of Southeast Asia called Kumandra, rich with color and cultural tropes. It’s a rainbow of blended areas from Thailand, to Myanmar to the Philippines. The story begins some 500 years ago when the denizens of Kumandra lived side by side with magnificent dragons. But, distressingly ominous black smoky orbs appear called the Druum and sweep through the five provinces turning to stone all they touch, including the dragons and humans. Only one dragon survives, Sisu (Awkwafina). Apparently all the dragons had transferred their power to one green gem, which defeated the Druum and was guarded by the province of Heart. Now, to the present: Heart still has the guardianship of the gem, though there exists a rivalry between the provinces for control of the sacred gem, now kept secure in a cellar vault. The Chief of Heart is Benji (Daniel Day Kim) who has trained Raya to be his warrior princess daughter. She has been given the task of acting as the protector of the magical gem. Benji, trying to unite the other four provinces, invites them to Heart for a feast. Unable to control the disagreement over who should keep the gem, a battle breaks out, and the gem is broken and Raya is betrayed by a close friend, Namari (Gamma Chan). Six years pass, and it’s at this point that the story takes hold. Raya sets off across Kumandra in search of the lone surviving dragon, Sisu, who could prove essential to restoring the gem and peace to her homeland. And on her journey she meets many interesting characters, finds Sisu, and tries to formulate (with the dragon’s help) a plan to restore the gem’s power and thereby protect all from the threat of the Druum. Raya and the Last Dragon is beautifully told and compellingly animated. Warrior princess Raya is a young, tenacious character, courageous and appealing. Girls and boys will enjoy her compelling adventure. Raya and the Last Dragon. Directed by Don Hall and Carlos Lopez Estrada. Disney animation studios. articles.text: Many people, myself included, tend to separate all of architecture into two large camps: traditional vs contemporary, sloped roofs vs flat roofs, ornamentation vs “clean” lines. This is what I call “the Great Divide.” Contemporary, or “modern”, is what we will touch upon today, and traditional is, well…everything else: from Spanish Revival to Tudor, to Craftsman to pretty much anything that appeared before the 1920s. In a nutshell, what happened is that in the early part of the 20th century, the development of new building materials and methods including structural steel, steel reinforced concrete, advanced roofing materials, and improved glazing (glass) production enabled engineers and architects to rapidly (over a few decades) develop and design buildings that were a complete departure from what the world had seen before. Interestingly, today, the way it is commonly used, “modern” is really a misnomer for a style type that is at least 100 years old now. Probably the most recognizable source of the “new” architecture, sometimes termed International Style, was the work of a number of famous modernists including Le Corbusier, Philip Johnson, and Mies van der Rohe. Their work was characterized by a rejection of the sentimentality of ornamented revivalist styles with instead the stated design goals of simplicity, clarity and “honesty” of structural expression. Close inspection of their work, however, often reveals ornamentation of a different kind as they sometimes employed unnecessary materials and detailing to make their buildings look more “machined” than they actually were. In any case, sharp clean lines, flat roofs, more use of metal materials, walls of large glass windows, exposed structural Just as in any traditional building, to be good architecture, contemporary styles must employ and enhance the same elements we have been discussing over the last months. Among these things are clarity and definition of a welcoming entry, proportion and harmony of the facades, well-detailed appropriate materials, and a strong relationship to the site and surrounding landscaping. steel and concrete were (and often continue to be) the result. In my opinion, one characteristic of this legitimate and sometimes beautiful style that inadvertently and ironically did itself a great disservice was precisely the unadorned, simple look. This evolved and proliferated into iterations and copies that were done minimally, were poorly crafted, and most of all, built cheaply—all justified by the structural “honesty” of the modern style. It is these compromised iterations on a large scale that people reject and react to as sterile and even ugly—often not a style at all, but the complete lack of any architectural style. Among a number of others, our friend Frank Lloyd Wright came to the rescue. He was apparently reluctant to venture into this world of modern architecture until demand required it, at which point he took it by storm. Unafraid of ornamentation and with his strong dedication to designing his buildings to harmonize with the land, he was instrumental in giving the “new” austere modern architecture another side: vitality, freshness, interest, character and soul. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com. Although probably very functional and certainly fire resistant, this modernist concrete and masonry structure lacks the texture, personality and appeal of many other more crafted styles. One reason is, I think, that unfinished concrete seems to naturally belong as a foundation or lower level material. articles.text: Garden column by Josh Harkinson Nothing is more controversial among California gardeners than the lawn. The cherished place to toss a baseball or roll out a picnic blanket, the lawn has also become a symbol of ecological callousness. According to a recent University of California study, lawns account for around 25 percent of residential water usage in California. With climate change predicted to increase the frequency and severity of droughts, we might not have that much water to spare in the future. But who wants to picnic on a bed of gravel or play croquet on bark mulch? Fortunately, there could be compromise: Native grasses have been growing in popularity for their beauty and ability to survive with little to no irrigation. I converted my lawn from traditional to native grass more than a decade ago. I felt very proud of myself at the time, but ten years later I’m still struggling with the transition. I’d suggest carefully considering the pros and cons before ripping up your sod. Among the many species of native and drought-tolerant grasses on the market, I know of only two that are tough and compact enough to walk on: festuca rubra (red fescue) and carex pansa (sand dune sedge). The fescue produces attractive clumps of thin, reddish-blue blades. It grows profusely in the East Bay hills – at least in places not taken over by invasive European grasses. of weeding to prevent invasive crab grass from swallowing up the natives, and a lot of water, so much that a neighbor reported me to EBMUD for wastage. (The agency declined to fine me after learning I was trying to establish drought-tolerant natives). After five years, 90 percent of the fescue had died. Although the carex pansa fared better, only half of it ended up surviving, mostly in the center of the yard where foot traffic was minimal. Over time, this critical mass gradually expanded. It now covers 70% of the yard and each year colonizes a few more square feet. It looks beautiful and stays green year-round with zero water. But maintaining it is tough. In the winter and spring, I yank out invasive crabgrass from the plot almost daily. It doesn’t tolerate foot traffic as well as a traditional lawn and needs sun for at least half the day. Though it can handle a picnic now and then, sitting on its inviting green clumps flattens them unattractively, so we mostly leave it to its own devices. At the end of the day, native grasses might be right for you if your lawn doesn’t get much footfall and you have the time or money to do a lot of weeding. But if you’re out there playing soccer or having lawn parties every weekend, you might consider holding on to your sod a bit longer. Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening. A close-up of carex pansa grass. Sand dune sedge, as its name suggests, grows in sand near to the ocean. It also doesn’t mind heavier soils. It spreads through rhizomes and puts up thick clumps of green, waxy leaves that extend a foot or more in length before falling into graceful tousles not unlike a surfer’s wavy hair. You can’t roll out a readymade lawn of native grasses as you can with traditional mats of sod. Their roots grow too deep. I purchased both varieties from the Bay Natives Nursery in San Francisco as plugs – big trays made up of hundreds of tiny pots each containing a miniscule blade of grass. Planting them, I felt like a hair replacement doctor as I spaced them out across the bare dirt and meticulously inserted a single plug at a time. Then I waited. . . for a very long time. Be careful what you wish for of weeding to prevent invasive crab grass from swallowing up the natives, and a lot of water, so much that a neighbor reported me to EBMUD for wastage. (The agency declined to fine me after learning I was trying to establish drought-tolerant natives). After five years, 90 percent of the fescue had died. Although the carex pansa fared better, only half of it ended up surviving, mostly in the center of the yard where foot traffic was minimal. Over time, this critical mass gradually expanded. It now covers 70% of the yard and each year colonizes a few more square feet. It looks beautiful and stays green year-round with zero water. But maintaining it is tough. In the winter and spring, I yank out invasive crabgrass from the plot almost daily. It doesn’t tolerate foot traffic as well as a traditional lawn and needs sun for at least half the day. Though it can handle a picnic now and then, sitting on its inviting green clumps flattens them unattractively, so we mostly leave it to its own devices. At the end of the day, native grasses might be right for you if your lawn doesn’t get much footfall and you have the time or money to do a lot of weeding. articles.text: Innocence battles evil while tensions run high and passions conflict in The Third Man, one of movie history’s most gripping thrillers. It’s been called “a masterpiece,” “unmissable” and “the best British film ever made.” Lucky local moviegoers can see it next week as the May offering of Piedmont’t Second Thursday Flix Fest. No wonder it’s such a success.Winning packed audiences and many awards when it was released in 1949, the screenplay is by novelist Graham Green, the director is the great Carol Reed, and its star is the prodigiously-talented Orson Welles. The film also features striking black-and-white cinematography by Robert Krasker, and its theme music, the haunting “Third Man Theme,” even became the number one song in the U.S. for a time. As the tale begins, an out-ofwork pulp fiction novelist, Holly Martins (Joseph Cotton), arrives in an edgy post-war Vienna divided into sectors by the victorious allies, where a shortage of supplies has led to a flourishing black market. He arrives at the invitation of an ex-school friend, Harry Lime (Orson Welles), who has offered him a job, only to discover that Lime has recently died in a peculiar traffic accident. From talking to Lime’s friends and associates, Martins soon notices that some of the stories are inconsistent – who is the mysterious “third man” who was present at Lime’s death? – and determines to discover what really happened. In the course of his pursuit he falls for Lime’s beautiful, heartbroken girlfriend, Anna (Alida Valli). The movie concludes with the famous chase through the Vienna sewers. On a perfect spring day last week the Walking on Wednesdays group had a large turnout of 53 walkers and four K-9 best friends. Many were there because architect and urban planner Will Adams was scheduled to lead the walk. Will is a 30-year Piedmonter and writes the Piedmont Post’s “Walking Piedmont” column. He took the walkers for a Mediterranean Style Architecture tour in February, and they wanted an encore. Will started the tour by providing an introduction to Craftsman style architecture. He told the group it is the most common architectural style in Piedmont. The Craftsman, or American Craftsman style, developed in tandem with the same style in England. Both are offshoots of the Arts and Crafts movement of the late 19th century, which idealized simplicity, harmony with nature and honesty in construction. It developed as an alternative to the ornate and opulent style of the Victorian age. Craftsman buildings were thoughtfully constructed by craftspeople who took pride in the quality of their work. The style is literally a blend of art and craft. Hand crafting of the building components both on the buildings’ exteriors and interiors is present and valued. Bernard Maybeck and his disciple Julia Morgan are among the famous architects who designed and worked closely with outstanding craftspeople to produce this type of buildings throughout the East Bay including Piedmont. Variations of this genre include the Craftsman Bungalow, the Prairie style and Mission Revival style. The large group went down Highland Avenue in what looked like an early 4th of July parade to Oakland Avenue and up to Hardwick Avenue. Will pointed to two Craftsman homes and pointed out similarities of natural colors, covered front porches, wide eaves and gables on lowsloped roofs, exposed rafters, double hung windows, brick chimneys and some stained glass windows. The tour resumed on Blair Avenue, crossing Oakland Avenue and then to two homes on Blair. One was a small bungalow, which Will said would have been inexpensive to build and very popular in California. Further down the street at Bonita Avenue was another Craftsman with its porch on the side. At Hillside Avenue was a larger Craftsman home with front steps that provided a setting for a group photo. The walkers continued to Dracena Avenue and to a lovely house where the architect has recreated a Craftsman style home with a porch at the front, and shingles, rocks and landscaping that complete the design. Will took the group into Dracena Park, emerging on Artuna and Ricardo Avenues where there are many Craftsman homes. The walkers expressed their thanks to Will for all the information he had shared. They are looking forward to another walk with Will later this year. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Dr. Joseph Yarris, a Piedmont resident for 60 years, passed away peacefully on Thanksgiving, November 23, 2023, with his family by his side. Born in Uniontown, Pennsylvania on February 24, 1932, to Joseph and Barbara Yarris, he was the youngest of three children. When he was in elementary school, his family moved to Vallejo, California, where he attended Vallejo College High School. He enrolled in the University of California at Berkeley as a freshman, with the intention of pursuing a career in medicine. After graduating from Cal, Joe continued his studies at McGill University Medical School in Montreal, Canada. There, he met the love of his life, Canadian Geraldine (Jere) O’Connell, at a party hosted by his fraternity. He was immediately captivated by Jere’s Irish wit, charm, and brilliant blue eyes. After dating for a year and a half, they became engaged, and, in 1957, exchanged wedding vows at the University Chapel on the McGill Campus. As newlyweds, the couple worked at the Royal Victoria Hospital, Joe as an intern and Jere as a receptionist in the Oncology/ Radiation Department. When Joe accepted a residency at Children’s Hospital in Oakland in 1960, they left Jere’s hometown of Montreal to begin a life in the San Francisco Bay Area. After the birth of two children and a few years as Oakland residents, they moved to Piedmont, where they would ultimately raise their five children. Upon completing his residency, Dr. Yarris began a private practice on “Pill Hill” in Oakland, partnered with mentors, Dr. Charles Dimmler and Dr. Bob Rappaport. He was a passionate pediatrician, and, with his reassuring bedside manner and a sense of humor, he easily earned the trust of his young patients and their parents. As a result, he affectionately became known as “Dr. Joe.” He spent many evenings on the phone with concerned mothers and fathers, made house calls, carrying his black bag, and was confident as Head of Pediatrics at Samuel Merritt Hospital (now Alta Bates Summit Medical Center). As his young patients matured, many were resistant to leaving their childhood physician, so Dr. Joe decided to expand his practice to include “Children and Young Adults”. Dr. Joe was a dedicated doctor with a hectic work schedule, but he was also a profoundly devoted husband and father, spending most of his free time with his children and wife. He was happiest in the outdoors with his family. He played with his children in the backyard, challenging them to games of football, ping-pong, basketball, and lively duels with water balloons and Nerf guns. He volunteered to coach his children’s sports teams, participated in weekend Scouting adventures and assisted in the construction of Pinewood Derby cars. Sundays often began with his smiley-faced pancakes and concluded with a bowl of Jiffy Pop popcorn and an evening episode of The Wonderful World of Disney. Family vacations usually involved a long station wagon ride to various California destinations – Tahoe, Palm Springs and Newport Beach among the favorites. Bikes, suitcases, and toys were stacked and tied to the rooftop of the car, while the inside was overcrowded with Yarris kids and their companions. Undeniably, Chambers Landing Beach, on the west shore of Lake Tahoe, was Dr. Joe’s most beloved location. He cherished time in the water, fishing for trout and crawdads from the pier with his kids and sharing a sunset cocktail on the Beach with Jere and their friends. Second to vacationing with his family, Joe loved being together for all holidays. The Christmas season was his favorite time of year. His lights and tree were always in place in time for the Piedmont Tree Lighting Ceremony. He was an enthusiastic shopper, a pro at assembling bikes and Barbie Dream Houses, and consistently overstuffed his kids’ and grandkids’ stockings. In 1998, when his third grandson was born at Summit Hospital, Dr. Joe performed his final newborn exam and retired from Pediatrics. In his newly acquired free time, he and Jere played tennis with friends, followed local sports teams, and discovered a love of cruising that took them to the Caribbean, Alaska, and Mexico. They took great pleasure relaxing at restaurants with water views: Sam’s in Sausalito, Quinn’s Lighthouse in Oakland, and Trader Vic’s in Emeryville for an “Old Way” Mai Tai as the sun was setting. They also spent time caring for their three young grandsons, who lived nearby in Piedmont. Just as with their own children, adventures with the boys were often outdoors: fishing from the Berkeley Pier and on the banks of Lake Temescal, and feeding the geese at Lake Merritt’s Lakeside Park. Dr. Joe’s appreciation of nature and outdoor activities cultivated his love of gardening. His patio was a sanctuary for squirrels and birds, as he enticed them daily with nuts and seeds. When he tended to his front garden, he was grateful when former patients and friends, who were walking or driving by his house, stopped to chat with him. He enjoyed reminiscing and hearing about family updates. In a quote from a 1975 article in an edition of the Piedmont High School newspaper, Dr. Yarris’ dedication to the well-being of children is undeniable. “Children are our most important investment in this world, and I feel that if we want them to grow up to be responsible citizens, we’ve just got to pass on every bit of knowledge we possibly can to make them strong and able to cope when we won’t be around to help them in their lives anymore,” he wrote. As a father, grandfather and Pediatrician, Dr. Joe undoubtedly helped generations of children become more confident and conscientious. Dr. Yarris is survived by his five children, Heather Yarris Price (Randy), Greg, Scott, Kevin, (Karyn), and Jennifer Mingham (Joe); seven grandchildren whom he adored: Brian, Matt and Nick Price, Cammi Yarris, and Andrew Dr. Joe Yarris toasting his 90th birthday with a Trader Vic’s Mai Tai. Joe and Jere Yarris on their wedding day. and Emily Mingham; his sister-inlaw, Wellner Gagnier; and many deeply loved nieces and nephews. Dr. Yarris was devoted to his Christian faith and profoundly believed in Heaven. In his happiest heaven, he would be surrounded by a garden, alongside his beloved Jere and others he’d missed, admiring a sunset. Donations in memory of Dr. Joseph Yarris may be made to: George Mark Children’s House, a local free-standing Pediatric respite care and hospice home (https://Georgemark.org) 2121 George Mark Lane, San Leandro, Ca. 94578). articles.text: Scouts from Piedmont’s Troop 15 welcomed new members with an introductory campout on the weekend of April 20-21 at Camp Herms in the hills of El Cerrito. The purpose was to provide hands-on practice of basic scout skills for youth who joined Troop 15 following the Piedmont Scout Troop Open House during the week of February 26. The new scouts received guidance from seasoned scouts selected by Senior Patrol Leader Evan Friedman. The instructor group included four scouts who themselves were new scouts at the same event two years prior – Willow Thomas, Henry Ciriacruz, Eliza Hupp and Adelina Mbize. The new scouts reviewed outdoor etiquette and scouting values, practiced tying basic knots, setting up a tent, handling a pocket knife, helping to prepare a meal, and cleaning up after the meal. New scout Adam Saxonov said he liked learning about knots and the Outdoor Code. The instruction went until late Saturday afternoon for each patrol of about seven scouts, after which they prepared dinner on two-burner propane camp stoves. After dinner, the whole Troop gathered around the campfire where each patrol put on a skit. Following the entertainment, the scouts toasted marshmallows over an open fire to make s’mores. Know that The Edge of Seventeen is not a collage of adolescent stereotypes; rather, it’s a film about fully-formed characters. Nadine is surrounded by a circle of caring friends and adults, to include her frazzled mom (Kyra Sedgwick). The narrative gradually morphs into is an attrition of Nadine’s anger and confusion, emotions that have turned her life into a roller coaster ride of hostility and all-consuming bewilderment. She loses her manic self-centeredness while she begins to gain small personal insights that come at her unexpectedly like small gifts. Who among us can forget what being 17 was like? What is there about being an adolescent that feels so real and involving? Will we ever live so intensely again, a time akin to walking on a high wire, framed by a sense of perpetual vertigo? It freaked me out.” Four police officers entered the business and informed the man that he was under arrest and instructed him to raise his hands. The suspect was unresponsive and muttering incoherently. An officer grabbed his taser and ordered him to get on the ground. When the suspect refused to comply, the officer used his taser, which did not incapacitate him. The man ripped the taser barbs from his skin and began flailing his arms violently at the cops. Additionally, tasers and pepper spray proved ineffective. The suspect fled down Grand Avenue onto Sunnyslope Avenue, where he broke a window to gain entry to a nearby house. He threatened its owner, who fled her home without injury. From there, he hopped a nearby fence and eventually landed in the front yard of a home on Valle Vista Avenue, where he encountered Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, alone Chief Bowers had been monitoring the situation via radio and arrived at the scene in plainclothes. He stopped his car in the middle of the street and opened the door to approach the man on foot. Bowers identified himself as a police officer. When the suspect noticed Bowers’ car door open, he sprinted toward the driver’s seat. Bowers attempted to remove the man from his car, resulting in a struggle. The ensuing melee stained the interior of the car with blood from the suspect’s hand which was cut due to breaking a window. Moments earlier, security guard Angel Solis was on duty at the Safeway on Grand Avenue when a distraught customer asked him for help. He just received a phone call that someone had broken into his house and threatened his wife. “He saw the first form of authority, which I guess he assumed was me in a bulletproof vest, and asked me if I could help him. Without waiting for an answer, he just took off down the road, so I followed,” said Solis. Solis encountered PPD Officers Tyler Petit and David Cutler on the street and offered his assistance. The two officers made contact with the suspect first. The suspect man stepped out of the car, swinging at the officers and still refusing orders. Solis approached the man from behind, bear-hugged him and dragged him to the ground. From there, he and two officers restrained the suspect while another officer handcuffed him. Piedmont Police have identified the suspect as 42-yearold Willie Gomer. Gomer was arrested on suspicion of assault, elder abuse, battery of a police officer, carjacking and burglary. Gomer was also on parole for auto theft, robbery, kidnapping and multiple parole violations. He was taken to the hospital for injuries to his hand and then booked at Santa Rita Jail in Dublin. Piedmont police are still awaiting toxicology reports to identify any substances Gomer may have been using. The assault victim at Ace Hardware was taken to the hospital and is expected to recover. Solis said he was glad he could help and praised the professionalism of Piedmont’s police. “The Chief actually came into my job, which is Safeway on Grand Avenue, and he personally handed me a letter of appreciation that he wrote, which benefits me a lot, because I’m currently [having background checks] with the SFPD.” A random assault took place at Ace Hardware on Friday, April 26.
